opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest challenge is access, and it comes in a few layers.

The most obvious one is access to the frontier models themselves. If crunch time means AI systems are roughly as capable as top human researchers at alignment, security, or policy analysis, the people who have those systems first, with the most compute and the fewest restrictions, will be inside the AI companies. An external group like Open Phil will be working with whatever's commercially available, which might lag the internal frontier by months. And in a world where things are moving fast, months could be the whole ballgame. So one thing I worry about is that the external ecosystem is always running a step behind, applying last generation's AI labor to this generation's problems.

The second layer is compute. Even with model access, scaling AI labor means running enormous numbers of copies of these systems for long stretches on hard research problems. That's expensive. Philanthropy is big in some absolute sense, but it's tiny next to what the labs and hyperscalers spend on compute. If the price of a unit of useful AI research labor stays high, or the best models are rationed, we could find ourselves with money to deploy and no good way to turn it into a lot of AI labor quickly.

The third layer, which I think gets underrated, is organizational readiness. Suppose you got the access and the compute tomorrow. Do you actually know what to point it at? Do you have the research agendas broken down into tasks AI systems can make progress on, plus the evaluation pipelines to tell whether the outputs are any good? A lot of safety and governance work is pretty pre-paradigmatic, and it's hard to verify. If you can't check the work, scaling up the labor might just scale up the noise, or worse, scale up subtly wrong results that look convincing.

So if I had to pick one, I'd say the deepest challenge is the verification and absorption problem: building the capacity, ahead of time, to productively direct and check huge amounts of AI labor. Access and compute you can at least imagine negotiating for, through partnerships with labs, government support, or compute set aside for safety work. Knowing what to do with it and trusting the results requires preparation that has to start now, before crunch time arrives. That's a big part of why I think it's worth investing today in figuring out which kinds of safety research are most automatable, and in getting people practiced at managing AI research assistants even while those assistants are still fairly limited.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier models will likely be held inside AI companies, while OpenPhil may only have access to commercially available models that lag behind.

r002.rationale: The response questions whether philanthropy could obtain enough compute, noting labs and hyperscalers outspend it and that compute or the best models may be rationed.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest challenge is that during crunch time, the labs are going to be the ones with the best models, the most compute, and the tightest feedback loops, and an external group like OpenPhil is structurally always going to be a step or two behind on all of those. So the question becomes: what's the thing that an outside group can actually do well, given that handicap?

My honest answer is that you can't really compete on raw capability. If the frontier labs have internally deployed systems that are substantially better than what's publicly available, and they're running them at enormous scale on their own research agendas, then whatever we're able to spin up with API access and a much smaller budget is going to look modest by comparison. And I think it's important to just be clear-eyed about that rather than imagining we're going to build some parallel research engine that matches them.

But I don't think that means an external group is irrelevant. I think the thing you can offer is independence and the freedom to work on questions the labs don't have strong incentives to prioritize. Evaluations that are adversarial to the labs' own interests, auditing work, trying to figure out whether the alignment research the automated systems are producing is actually trustworthy or whether it's subtly steering toward conclusions the models prefer. Those are things where being outside the building is a feature rather than a bug.

The practical challenges are pretty mundane, though. It's hard to get access to the models that matter. It's hard to hire people who can manage large fleets of AI agents well, because that's a skill that barely existed a couple years ago and the people who have it are getting paid a lot more at the labs. It's hard to know whether the work you're funding is any good when it's being produced faster than any human can review it. And there's a real organizational risk of either moving too slowly because you're being careful, or moving too fast and ending up as a kind of rubber stamp for whatever the systems produce.

So I'd say the biggest single challenge is figuring out how to be genuinely useful rather than symbolically useful. It's very easy for an outside group to end up doing things that feel important but don't actually change any decisions. And in a world where the stakes are rising quickly and the timelines are compressed, I think we have to be pretty ruthless about asking whether a given project is going to matter or whether it's just letting us feel like we're participating.

r001.rationale: The response says access to the models that matter is difficult and that outside groups rely on API access while labs have better internally deployed systems.

r002.rationale: It notes that labs have more compute and outside groups have smaller budgets, but does not address whether the group could obtain enough compute hardware amid competing demand.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest challenge is that access to AI labor isn’t the same as being able to use it effectively. You need to know what work to assign, give the systems the relevant context, and tell whether what they produce is actually good. And those tasks can still depend on a relatively small number of people with a lot of judgment and institutional knowledge.

So if things are moving very quickly, I worry that we could have access to a huge amount of AI labor and still have a bottleneck in our ability to direct it. For an external organization like OpenPhil, there’s also the question of how quickly we get access to the capabilities that the labs are already using internally.

That makes me think a lot of the preparation has to happen ahead of time: experimenting with delegation, figuring out how to evaluate outputs, and making the context for our work easier to share. You don’t want to be learning all of that for the first time during crunch time.

r001.rationale: The response raises whether OpenPhil can get access to capabilities the labs are already using internally, which communicates concern about access to the best models during crunch time.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention compute hardware or competing demand for it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest challenge is that having access to a lot of AI labor isn’t the same as knowing how to use it effectively. You need to figure out what work to delegate, give the AIs enough context, and evaluate whether they’ve actually done a good job. And those things can require time from the very people whose time you’re trying to save.

For an external group like OpenPhil, that’s compounded by being farther from the frontier labs. We might not have access to the same systems or the same information about what those systems can do. So I’d be worried about a situation where, in principle, there’s this enormous amount of useful labor available, but we haven’t built the workflows or the judgment to turn it into useful output quickly. That seems like a reason to start experimenting before crunch time, when there’s still room to learn.

r001.rationale: It says an external group might not have access to the same systems as frontier labs, which clearly raises doubt about access to the best models.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention compute hardware or whether competing demand could limit access to it.
